tagline: Two great marshes on the Central Flyway, joined by county roads.
intro: From Hoisington, on the southern edge of the Smoky Hills, the byway runs east on K-4 past Cheyenne Bottoms, a natural sink of some 41,000 acres and the largest wetland in the interior United States. Then it turns south on county roads, with a few miles of K-156, to Quivira National Wildlife Refuge and on to St. John. Millions of migrating birds stop along it each year, whooping cranes among them.

Water has always been the question at the Bottoms. A ditch dug in 1900 to bring in the Arkansas River washed out in a flood. In the 1920s there were plans to drain the place for farmland, until Hutchinson, downstream, protested that it would be flooded.

moments.title: Cheyenne Bottoms
moments.text: Blood Creek, named for a legendary battle of 1825 that turned it red, still flows into the marsh, and American greyhound racing traces its start to a coursing event here in 1886.

moments.title: Quivira National Wildlife Refuge
moments.text: Named for the city of gold Coronado came looking for in 1541 and never found, the refuge keeps salt marshes, a 14-mile wildlife road and an observation tower on Little Salt Marsh.

moments.title: St. John
moments.text: Founded in 1875 as a religious colony called Zion Valley, the town renamed itself after the governor in 1879 to help win the county seat, which it holds today.

practical: Much of the route is on county roads. Watch the signs at K-156 and west of Quivira, where the byway's own directions call the turns tricky.
